The Spanish Shylock Problem
One of the definitions of the Spanish word for Jew, “judío,” in the official dictionary of the Royal Spanish Academy, is “a miserly or usurious person.” In 2024 an Argentine judge ordered the Academy, which is based in Madrid, to remove the definition, following a campaign by Jewish organizations in Latin America.
The Academy refused. If the official dictionary defines “Jew” as “miserly,” it is because that’s how people use the word, said Santiago Muñoz Machado, the Academy’s director. Two years later, the dictionary retains that definition, while acknowledging that it is considered offensive.
Beware of old false beliefs, which take a very long time to die and continue to cause trouble. Look at Donald Trump, a self-professed anti-antisemite, who repeatedly evoked the image of Shakespeare’s Shylock, one of literature’s most antisemitic tropes, during the midterm campaign.
In part, this reflects the debate over the role of dictionaries in society. Are they a snapshot of daily speech or do they tell society how to use words? Are the makers of dictionaries responsible for the views expressed in them? Who decides what a definition should be?
Since its inception in 1713, the Royal Spanish Academy — its motto used to be “clean, fix and give splendor” — has legislated the Spanish language’s orthography (proper spelling, for example), syntax and punctuation. Mostly it keeps in its dictionary the words it believes speakers should use and rejects those it deems unworthy. Its reputation is snobbish: Many see its imperious behavior as the reflection of a self-proclaimed supreme, implacable authority. That it is compiled in Spain often infuriates people in Latin America, who feel the language is as much theirs, if not more, based on the number of speakers.
To that end, frustratingly, Mr. Muñoz Machado told the news media that an Argentine judge has no jurisdiction over the Academy’s dictionary.
